newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan envoy to Peru now a disgraced hero.
newsitem.headline: Japan envoy to Peru now a disgraced hero.

text.p: Initially hailed as a hero who defended fellow hostages from Marxist rebels for months, Japan's Ambassador to Peru Morihisa Aoki fell from grace on Tuesday when he was relieved of his post.
Aoki, 58, hosted a reception at his residence in Lima last December 17 that was stormed by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels who took hundreds of guests hostage.

Although the drama ended last month when Peruvian commandos freed all but one of the remaining 72 hostages, Aoki's ordeal went on with questioning about what responsibility he should bear for security lapses that allowed the siege to happen.
On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda unexpectedly announced during parliamentary questioning of Aoki that the government had decided to accept his resignation as ambassador to Peru.
Aoki, who was sitting beside Ikeda in the hearing, showed no emotion or surprise at the announcement.

Aoki has denied that he was forewarned of a terrorist attack or that the Peruvian government had offered to tighten security around the residence on the day of the reception, two allegations against him widely reported in the Japanese media.

His departure signalled the end of a career for an ambassador who was closely linked by his family to Latin America. Aoki's father and grandfather were both also well-known Japanese diplomats to the region.
A descendant of samurai, Japan's traditional warrior class, Aoki lived up to his heritage when the rebels stormed his residence during a glittering party celebrating the birthday of Japan's emperor.
While the rebels sprayed the inside of the the building with gunfire and guests dived to the floor, Aoki stood upright, appealing to them to stop shooting.
He offered several times to remain with the rebels as a willing hostage if they would release all other captives.
During the long days of the four-month siege, hostages credited Aoki with keeping up their spirits and morale and striking up a dialogue with the rebels that kept the captives from harm.
In the commando raid that killed all 14 rebels, Aoki injured his hips and legs when he jumped for safety after trying to ensure that all the hostages were out of harm's way.
One hostage and two soldiers died in the raid.
Things started to turn sour for the courtly, silver-haired Aoki when he returned to Japan and the spotlight swung from the fate of the hostages to why the incident happened.
In Japan's carefully mannered society, he lost points by chain smoking during a news conference and antagonised some media with abrasive answers to questions.
Some Japanese legislators also complained that Aoki's initial apology to the nation for the inadequate of security was not fulsome enough.
It is not clear when Aoki's resignation will take effect or if he will remain in Japan's diplomatic service.
Prior to his Peru assignment, Aoki was a senior official of the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), the aid arm of the Foreign Ministry.
He also served as a deputy foreign minister and chief of the ministry's intelligence and research bureau.

After passing the senior civil servant exam in 1962 from the elite Tokyo University, he joined the Foreign Ministry in 1963 and served at Japanese embassies in the Philippines, Hong Kong and the United Nations.
Aoki's wife Naoko was with him at the reception when the guerrillas attacked but she was later freed. They have a son, who said after the hostages' release that he was proud of his father.
